solution: The learners were asked {=asked}, and every answer is a name or a word, not a number. The data set cannot be written as numbers, so it is qualitative.

It is not anecdotal: no response is a story, and it does not matter that the answers come from the learners themselves. It is not quantitative either: counting how many learners gave each answer does not turn the answers into numbers.
Therefore the data set is qualitative categorical, because the responses are not numbers and each one comes from a limited set of possibilities.

families.stem: A teacher asks the learners in her class two questions and records the answers as two data sets. Data set 1 holds the answers to this question: {=q1} The answers were: "{=d1[0]}"; "{=d1[1]}"; "{=d1[2]}"; "{=d1[3]}". choices.correct: Data set 1 is qualitative {=t1} and data set 2 is qualitative {=t2}.

distractors.text: Both data sets are qualitative anecdotal, because both sets of answers come from the learners themselves.
Both data sets are qualitative categorical, because both are made of words.
Data set 1 is qualitative {=t2} and data set 2 is qualitative {=t1}.

solution: Neither data set can be written as numbers, so both are qualitative.
In data set {=cn} the answers are picked from a limited set of possibilities: only three different answers appear, and some learners gave the same one. So data set {=cn} is categorical.
In data set {=an} each learner answered in a sentence of his or her own, in the form of a story, so data set {=an} is anecdotal.

Both data sets come from the same learners, so where the answers come from cannot tell the two types apart. It is the form of the answers that decides: words picked from a limited set are categorical, and sentences in the learners' own words are anecdotal.
Therefore data set {=cn} is qualitative categorical and data set {=an} is qualitative anecdotal.

families.stem: The following is a list of data: ${=a}; {=b}; {=c}; {=d}; {=e}; x$. Determine the value of $x$ if the mean of all six values is ${=m}$.
solution: The mean is the sum of the values divided by how many values there are. This list has 6 values, counting $x$.
Add the values we know: ${=a}+{=b}+{=c}+{=d}+{=e}={=known}$. The sum of all six values is therefore $x+{=known}$.
Put this into the mean: $\begin{aligned}{=m}&=\frac{x+{=known}}{6}\\x+{=known}&={=m}\times 6\\x+{=known}&={=total}\end{aligned}$
Subtract ${=known}$ from both sides: $\begin{aligned}x&={=total}-{=known}\\x&={=u}\end{aligned}$
Check: $\frac{{=known}+{=u}}{6}=\frac{{=total}}{6}={=m}$, so $x={=u}$ gives the mean ${=m}$.
families.notes: Basic-tier entry point of the skill, modelled on book question ex10-7-25d (list of data with an unknown x, mean given, page 387; book answer 10 from x + 38 = 48). families.stem: A group of $20$ learners count the number of stones they each have. This is the data they collect: $\begin{aligned}\begin{array}{ccccc} {=d1}&{=d2}&{=d3}&{=d4}&{=d5} \\ {=d6}&{=d7}&{=d8}&{=d9}&{=d10} \\ {=d11}&{=d12}&{=d13}&{=d14}&{=d15} \\ {=d16}&{=d17}&{=d18}&{=d19}&{=d20} \end{array}\end{aligned}$ Group the data into these four ranges and draw a histogram: ${=l1}\le\text{number of stones}\le {=h1}$, ${=l2}\le\text{number of stones}\le {=h2}$, ${=l3}\le\text{number of stones}\le {=h3}$ and ${=l4}\le\text{number of stones}\le {=h4}$. How many more learners are in the tallest bar of the histogram than in the shortest bar?
solution: Firstly, sort the data from the smallest value to the largest.

Secondly, count how many of the sorted values fall in each range. A value on the edge of a range belongs to that range, because the signs are $\le$. Each count is the height of one bar of the histogram.

${=l1}\le\text{number of stones}\le {=h1}$: {=f1} learners; ${=l2}\le\text{number of stones}\le {=h2}$: {=f2} learners; ${=l3}\le\text{number of stones}\le {=h3}$: {=f3} learners; ${=l4}\le\text{number of stones}\le {=h4}$: {=f4} learners.
Check: ${=f1}+{=f2}+{=f3}+{=f4}=20$, so every learner is counted in exactly one bar.
The tallest bar is {=mx} learners high and the shortest bar is {=mn} learners high.
${=mx}-{=mn}={=mx - mn}$, so the tallest bar has {=mx - mn} more learners than the shortest bar.
families.notes: Advanced tier: the book's standard items (ex10-3-3/4, ex10-7-12/13) ask for ONE range of an unsorted 4x5 grid of 20 counts. Here the learner must group ALL 20 values into four given equal-width ranges (the book's inclusive form a <= number <= b), i.e. build the whole grouped frequency table, then compare the tallest and shortest bars: several steps, same method (sort, group, read the bar heights). Instances vary: start s in {0,1} and width w in {4,5} give ranges 0-3..12-15, 1-4..13-16, 0-4..15-19 or 1-5..16-20; the 20 data values are drawn independently and uniformly inside the four ranges, so repeats and edge values (e.g. 5, 6, 10, 11) are common, as in the book. Requires: every bar non-empty, a unique tallest and a unique shortest bar (so the wording names one bar each), and a gap of at most 8. The answer is the integer difference of the two heights, never a decimal. Counts were checked in a separate simulation against an independent bucketing (v - s) // w; the four counts always sum to 20. No distractors (numeric). The catalogued mc:g10m10s3-1-1:boundary-value-in-wrong-range is the likely wrong-answer source (an edge value placed in the neighbouring bar) but cannot be tagged on a typed numeric answer; the solution's step 3 states the edge rule explicitly.

families.stem: Alfred runs a minibus taxi. Over {=n} weeks he counted the passengers he carried each week and sorted the weekly totals into groups, where $x$ is the number of passengers in a week: ${=lo[0]}<x\leq{=lo[1]}$ in {=cs[0]} weeks; ${=lo[1]}<x\leq{=lo[2]}$ in {=cs[1]} weeks; ${=lo[2]}<x\leq{=lo[3]}$ in {=cs[2]} weeks; ${=lo[3]}<x\leq{=lo[4]}$ in {=cs[3]} weeks; ${=lo[4]}<x\leq{=lo[5]}$ in {=cs[4]} weeks; ${=lo[5]}<x\leq{=lo[6]}$ in {=cs[5]} weeks. Estimate how much money Alfred made over these {=n} weeks by treating every week in a group as having the number of passengers at the centre of that group. Assume that every passenger travelled an average of {=d} $\text{km}$ and that Alfred charged R{=fixed(rc / 100, 2)} per $\text{km}$. Give your answer in rand.
solution: Treat every week in a group as having the number of passengers at the centre of its group. The centres of the six groups are {=mids[0]}, {=mids[1]}, {=mids[2]}, {=mids[3]}, {=mids[4]} and {=mids[5]}.

Multiply each count of weeks by the centre of its group and add, to estimate the total number of passengers: ${=cs[0]}({=mids[0]})+{=cs[1]}({=mids[1]})+{=cs[2]}({=mids[2]})+{=cs[3]}({=mids[3]})+{=cs[4]}({=mids[4]})+{=cs[5]}({=mids[5]})={=total}$ passengers.
Each passenger travelled {=d} $\text{km}$ at R{=fixed(rc / 100, 2)} per $\text{km}$, so each passenger paid ${=d}\times{=fixed(rc / 100, 2)}={=per}$ rand.
The estimated takings are ${=total}\times{=per}={=takings}$, so Alfred made about R{=takings}.

Counts are drawn as 6 distinct values from 2..11 so a group is never empty. d is even and the rate is a multiple of R0.50, so the fare per passenger is always a whole number of rand and the answer is a whole number (about 150 000 to 1 200 000, the book's own is 588 000). The Rand is kept as in the book. Only the estimate under the centre-of-group rule is asked for, and the stem states that rule, so a solver cannot take the exact total.

families.stem: Alfred runs a minibus taxi. Over {=n} weeks he counted the passengers he carried each week and sorted the weekly totals into groups, where $x$ is the number of passengers in a week: ${=lo[0]}<x\leq{=lo[1]}$ in {=cs[0]} weeks; ${=lo[1]}<x\leq{=lo[2]}$ in {=cs[1]} weeks; ${=lo[2]}<x\leq{=lo[3]}$ in {=cs[2]} weeks; ${=lo[3]}<x\leq{=lo[4]}$ in {=cs[3]} weeks; ${=lo[4]}<x\leq{=lo[5]}$ in {=cs[4]} weeks; ${=lo[5]}<x\leq{=lo[6]}$ in {=cs[5]} weeks. Treat every week in a group as having the number of passengers at the centre of that group. Estimate the mean number of passengers per week, and estimate the median as the centre of the median group (the group that contains the middle value). Calculate the difference between these two estimates, that is, the larger estimate minus the smaller one.
solution: Treat every week in a group as having the number of passengers at the centre of its group. The centres of the six groups are {=mids[0]}, {=mids[1]}, {=mids[2]}, {=mids[3]}, {=mids[4]} and {=mids[5]}.
Estimate the total number of passengers: ${=cs[0]}({=mids[0]})+{=cs[1]}({=mids[1]})+{=cs[2]}({=mids[2]})+{=cs[3]}({=mids[3]})+{=cs[4]}({=mids[4]})+{=cs[5]}({=mids[5]})={=total}$.
There are {=n} weeks, so the estimated mean is ${=total}\div{=n}={=mean}$ passengers per week.

For the median, there are {=n} values, so the median lies between the {=lowpos}th and {=highpos}th values. Adding the counts group by group gives the cumulative counts {=cum[0]}, {=cum[1]}, {=cum[2]}, {=cum[3]}, {=cum[4]} and {=cum[5]}. The cumulative count first reaches {=lowpos} in the group ${=lo[g]}<x\leq{=lo[g + 1]}$ and is {=cum[g]} by the end of it, so the {=lowpos}th and {=highpos}th values both lie in this group. This is the median group.
The estimated median is the centre of the median group: {=med}.
The difference between the estimates is ${=max(mean, med)}-{=min(mean, med)}={=diff}$ passengers.
families.notes: Mirrors book Ex 10.4 Q3(c) and (d): estimate of the mean from count x centre, and estimate of the median as the middle value (centre) of the median group, then compare the two. Six groups of width 100 written as a < x <= b with the counts as numbers of weeks, as in the histogram. n is 20 or 50 (a divisor of 100), so the estimated mean is always a whole number; n is even so the median lies between the (n/2)th and (n/2+1)th values and the family requires both to fall in one group, which keeps the median group unambiguous. Counts are made from 5 sorted cut points, so every group has at least 1 week and they total n; a single modal group is required. The stem states the median-estimate rule used by the book (centre of the median group), so a solver is not asked to interpolate. The mean-minus-median sign can go either way, so the stem asks for the larger minus the smaller.

families.stem: A group of $10$ learners count the number of marbles they each have. This is the data they collect: $\left\{ {=s[0]}, {=s[1]}, {=s[2]}, {=s[3]}, {=s[4]}, {=s[5]}, {=s[6]}, {=s[7]}, {=s[8]}, {=s[9]} \right\}$ Find the range of the data set. Then find by how much the range decreases when the value ${=out}$, which is not typical of the other values, is removed from the data set. Give this decrease in the range as your answer.
solution: Put the data set in order, from the smallest value to the largest: $\left\{ {=fs[0]}, {=fs[1]}, {=fs[2]}, {=fs[3]}, {=fs[4]}, {=fs[5]}, {=fs[6]}, {=fs[7]}, {=fs[8]}, {=fs[9]} \right\}$
The maximum value is ${=mx}$ and the minimum value is ${=mn}$.
The range is the maximum value minus the minimum value: $\text{range} = {=mx} - {=mn} = {=rng1}$.

The value ${=out}$ is not typical of the other values, so remove it. The data set that is left is $\left\{ {=cs[0]}, {=cs[1]}, {=cs[2]}, {=cs[3]}, {=cs[4]}, {=cs[5]}, {=cs[6]}, {=cs[7]}, {=cs[8]} \right\}$
In this new data set the maximum value is ${=cmax}$ and the minimum value is ${=cmin}$, so the new range is ${=cmax} - {=cmin} = {=rng2}$.
The range goes from ${=rng1}$ to ${=rng2}$, so it decreases by ${=rng1} - {=rng2} = {=drop}$. The value ${=out}$ is an outlier and has a big influence on the range.
families.notes: Advanced = the book's we10 twist (remove a value that is not typical, see the range change) joined to the ex10-7-18 style of data: ten UNORDERED values, order them, find max and min, find the range, remove the outlier, find the new range, take the difference. Whole data set is shuffled so the outlier sits anywhere in the list. The outlier (low or high, by 'side') is always the unique extreme: core values lie in a window of width 10 and the outlier is 12 to 19 beyond the nearest core extreme, so after removal the new max and min are unambiguous. Marbles cannot be negative: base >= 20 and gap <= 19 keep the low outlier at 1 or more. The decrease always equals the gap (checked by the constraint drop == gap); a solver who shortcuts to the gap still gets the right answer. The answer is the decrease only, one whole number, so there is no two-part marker. No distractors (numeric).

What happens to the range of the data set if the first value is removed?
solution: Put the data set in order, from the smallest value to the largest: $\left\{ {=fs[0]}, {=fs[1]}, {=fs[2]}, {=fs[3]}, {=fs[4]}, {=fs[5]}, {=fs[6]}, {=fs[7]} \right\}$
The maximum value is ${=mx}$ and the minimum value is ${=mn}$, so the range is ${=mx} - {=mn} = {=rng1}$.
Remove the first value, ${=out}$. The data set that is left, in order, is $\left\{ {=cs[0]}, {=cs[1]}, {=cs[2]}, {=cs[3]}, {=cs[4]}, {=cs[5]}, {=cs[6]} \right\}$
The new maximum value is ${=cmax}$ and the new minimum value is ${=cmin}$, so the new range is ${=cmax} - {=cmin} = {=rng2}$.

The range decreases from ${=rng1}$ to ${=rng2}$. The value ${=out}$ is not typical of the other values: it is an outlier, and it has a big influence on the range because the range depends only on the largest and the smallest value.

distractors.text: The range stays at ${=rng1}$, because only one of the values is removed.

The range decreases by $1$, from ${=rng1}$ to ${=rng1 - 1}$.

families.stem: A company wanted to evaluate the training programme in its factory. They gave the same task to trained and untrained employees and timed each one in seconds. Trained: ${=tdata[0]}, {=tdata[1]}, {=tdata[2]}, {=tdata[3]}, {=tdata[4]}, {=tdata[5]}, {=tdata[6]}, {=tdata[7]}, {=tdata[8]}, {=tdata[9]}, {=tdata[10]}$ Untrained: ${=udata[0]}, {=udata[1]}, {=udata[2]}, {=udata[3]}, {=udata[4]}, {=udata[5]}, {=udata[6]}, {=udata[7]}, {=udata[8]}, {=udata[9]}, {=udata[10]}$ Take the lower quartile as the median of the lower half of the ordered data and the upper quartile as the median of the upper half; when there is an odd number of values, the median belongs to both halves. By how many seconds is the semi-interquartile range of the untrained employees greater than that of the trained employees?
solution: Arrange the trained times in ascending order: ${=tsort[0]}, {=tsort[1]}, {=tsort[2]}, {=tsort[3]}, {=tsort[4]}, {=tsort[5]}, {=tsort[6]}, {=tsort[7]}, {=tsort[8]}, {=tsort[9]}, {=tsort[10]}$.

There are 11 trained times, so the median is the 6th value. It belongs to both halves, so each half has 6 values. The lower quartile is the median of the 1st to 6th values, the average of the 3rd and 4th: $Q_1=\frac{{=tsort[2]}+{=tsort[3]}}{2}={=tq1}$. The upper quartile is the median of the 6th to 11th values, the average of the 8th and 9th: $Q_3=\frac{{=tsort[7]}+{=tsort[8]}}{2}={=tq3}$.
The semi-interquartile range is half the interquartile range: $\frac{Q_3-Q_1}{2}=\frac{{=tq3}-{=tq1}}{2}={=tsiqr}$ seconds for the trained employees.
Arrange the untrained times in ascending order: ${=usort[0]}, {=usort[1]}, {=usort[2]}, {=usort[3]}, {=usort[4]}, {=usort[5]}, {=usort[6]}, {=usort[7]}, {=usort[8]}, {=usort[9]}, {=usort[10]}$.

There are 11 untrained times, so the median is the 6th value. It belongs to both halves, so each half has 6 values. The lower quartile is the median of the 1st to 6th values, the average of the 3rd and 4th: $Q_1=\frac{{=usort[2]}+{=usort[3]}}{2}={=uq1}$. The upper quartile is the median of the 6th to 11th values, the average of the 8th and 9th: $Q_3=\frac{{=usort[7]}+{=usort[8]}}{2}={=uq3}$.
The semi-interquartile range is half the interquartile range: $\frac{Q_3-Q_1}{2}=\frac{{=uq3}-{=uq1}}{2}={=usiqr}$ seconds for the untrained employees.
Subtract: $\text{untrained}-\text{trained}={=usiqr}-{=tsiqr}={=diff}$ seconds.
families.notes: Models ex10-7-22b (trained vs untrained times) and extends it: the book finds the interquartile range of both unsorted sets; here the learner finds the semi-interquartile range of both and compares them. constraints: x1 < x2 and x2 < x4 and x4 < x6 and x6 < x7
families.stem: The data set below is already in order, from smallest to largest. $\left\{ {=x1}, {=x2}, {=x3}, {=x4}, {=x5}, {=x6}, {=x7} \right\}$ Give the five number summary (minimum, $Q_1$, median, $Q_3$, maximum), in that order. Use the percentile formula to find the quartiles: the $p$th percentile lies at position $\frac{p}{100} \times n$, where $n$ is the number of values; round this position up to the next whole number. $Q_1$, the median and $Q_3$ are the 25th, 50th and 75th percentiles.
solution: The data set is already in order, so the minimum is the first value, ${=x1}$, and the maximum is the last value, ${=x7}$.
There are $n = 7$ values. The median is the 50th percentile: $\frac{50}{100} \times 7 = 3.5$, which rounds up to 4. The median is the 4th value, ${=x4}$.
$Q_1$ is the 25th percentile: $\frac{25}{100} \times 7 = 1.75$, which rounds up to 2. $Q_1$ is the 2nd value, ${=x2}$.
$Q_3$ is the 75th percentile: $\frac{75}{100} \times 7 = 5.25$, which rounds up to 6. $Q_3$ is the 6th value, ${=x6}$.
The five number summary is: minimum ${=x1}$, $Q_1 = {=x2}$, median ${=x4}$, $Q_3 = {=x6}$, maximum ${=x7}$.
families.notes: Entry point: seven values, already ordered, no context, so the student only has to locate the five positions (1st, 2nd, 4th, 6th, 7th). All values are whole numbers and strictly increasing, so the five summary values are always distinct and the key is a clean ascending list. The stem states the percentile-position rule (round the position up) because the book's own stem leaves it implicit and a blind solver otherwise has to choose between this rule, (n+1)p/100 interpolation, median-of-halves and spreadsheet interpolation, which disagree on some sizes. Only an odd number of values is used, so a quartile position is never a whole number and the book's treatment of a whole-number position (not shown in the single book solution I was given) is never needed.

solution: First arrange the 13 values in order, from smallest to largest. A value that occurs more than once is written each time it occurs (here ${=x5}$ appears twice). $\left\{ {=xs[0]}, {=xs[1]}, {=xs[2]}, {=xs[3]}, {=xs[4]}, {=xs[5]}, {=xs[6]}, {=xs[7]}, {=xs[8]}, {=xs[9]}, {=xs[10]}, {=xs[11]}, {=xs[12]} \right\}$
The minimum is the first value, ${=x1}$, and the maximum is the last value, ${=x13}$.
There are $n = 13$ values. The median is the 50th percentile: $\frac{50}{100} \times 13 = 6.5$, which rounds up to 7. The median is the 7th value, ${=x7}$.
$Q_1$ is the 25th percentile: $\frac{25}{100} \times 13 = 3.25$, which rounds up to 4. $Q_1$ is the 4th value, ${=x4}$.
$Q_3$ is the 75th percentile: $\frac{75}{100} \times 13 = 9.75$, which rounds up to 10. $Q_3$ is the 10th value, ${=x10}$.
The five number summary is: minimum ${=x1}$, $Q_1 = {=x4}$, median ${=x7}$, $Q_3 = {=x10}$, maximum ${=x13}$.
families.notes: Advanced: the book's own twist (raw, unordered data in a context, with a repeated value) at a larger size, 13 values, so the student must order the data and then locate positions 4, 7 and 10 from rounded-up percentile positions (3.25, 6.5, 9.75). The data are built already sorted (xs), then shuffled for display (s); the key and the solution use the sorted list. A repeated value is guaranteed (x5 = x6, strictly between x4 and x7, so it occurs exactly twice) and further ties occur at random. The strict gaps x3<x4, x6<x7, x9<x10 and x10<x11 are there so that the usual wrong answers (rounding down to positions 3, 6, 9, or (n+1)p/100 interpolation giving the mean of the 3rd and 4th, and of the 10th and 11th) never coincide with the correct value, and so the five summary values are always distinct. families.stem: A box-and-whisker plot is drawn above a number line. The box runs from ${=b}$ to ${=d}$, and a line inside the box is drawn at ${=c}$. solution: The whiskers show where the minimum and maximum values lie. The left whisker starts at ${=a}$ and the right whisker ends at ${=e}$, so the minimum is ${=a}$ and the maximum is ${=e}$.
The box shows the interquartile range: its two ends are $Q_1$ and $Q_3$. The box runs from ${=b}$ to ${=d}$, so $Q_1 = {=b}$ and $Q_3 = {=d}$.
The line inside the box shows the median. It is drawn at ${=c}$, so the median is ${=c}$.

solution: The question is about plot $B$ only. The number ${=mdB}$ also appears in plot $A$, but there it marks a different part of the plot, so plot $A$ does not help.
